clue.text: Facilities some use in drought (but some non-smokers cannot)

definitions.meaning: street water taps set up when household supplies are cut off in a dry spell
read as a phrase, what a non-smoker cannot do is put up with briar and clay smoking things

explanation.surface: A remark about drought-time water supplies, with a jokey aside about people who dislike tobacco.
explanation.walkthrough: Split the answer as a verb phrase: some non-smokers cannot tolerate (stand) tobacco smokers' implements (pipes).
explanation.definitionFit: Standpipes are temporary street taps that households queue at when the mains are rationed in a drought.

clue.text: Turkish chief's rise. It's a long story

indicators.note: in a down clue rise means the letters go upward, read from bottom to top

parts.note: an aga is a Turkish chief or commander, here with possessive s

explanation.surface: The rise of a Turkish leader is a lengthy tale.
explanation.definitionFit: A saga is a long heroic narrative, originally Norse.

clue.text: Greed involving caviare

indicators.note: involving suggests letters wound up and entangled, so rearrange the fish roe word

explanation.surface: Greed when it comes to expensive fish eggs.
explanation.definitionFit: Avarice is an extreme desire for wealth, a synonym of greed.

clue.text: What Heber's, Ceylon would have been, de-vilified?

definitions.text: What Heber's, Ceylon would have been, de-vilified?

parts.words: What Heber's, Ceylon would have been, de-vilified?
parts.note: Bishop Heber's hymn says of Ceylon that 'only man is vile'; take away the vile one and the place is uninhabited

explanation.surface: A question about a hymn writer's tropical island stripped of wickedness.
explanation.walkthrough: Heber's missionary hymn 'From Greenland's Icy Mountains' says every prospect pleases and only man is vile: remove man and no one lives there.
explanation.definitionFit: An uninhabited island has no people, which is what Ceylon would be without its vile humans.

clue.text: Ship protected from ravages of cold rain

indicators.note: ravages wreck and churn things, so these letters are scrambled

explanation.surface: A vessel sheltered from the harm done by a cold downpour.
explanation.definitionFit: An ironclad is a 19th-century warship armoured with iron plates.

clue.text: Relaxing what. 26 is in for example

indicators.note: in says the description of entry 26 goes inside the abbreviation for for example

parts.note: EG abbreviates exempli gratia, for example
26 across is one of the seven deadly sins, so it is a sin

explanation.surface: Unwinding, with a cross-reference to another clue.
explanation.definitionFit: Easing means loosening or slackening, the same as letting up.

clue.text: Fly past

parts.note: looks like an aircraft display, but asks for the past tense of the verb to fly

explanation.walkthrough: A flypast is an aerial display; read instead as 'the past of fly'.
explanation.definitionFit: Grammatical relation: the simple past tense form of the verb meaning to travel through the air.

clue.text: Spot-on target in the jungle ?

parts.note: spot-on is read as covered in spots, describing a big cat a hunter aims at in the forest

explanation.surface: A perfectly accurate bullseye somewhere deep in the jungle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spot-on' means precise, but split it: a target with spots on it.
explanation.definitionFit: The leopard is a big cat with a spotted coat, hunted as big game.

clue.text: What governors, must do, or slow down

definitions.meaning: those who govern must labour at ruling
industrial action in which workers follow every regulation to cut output

explanation.surface: The duties of rulers, or a go-slow by workers.
explanation.walkthrough: A work-to-rule is British industrial action: staff obey every regulation strictly so output slows.
explanation.definitionFit: Rulers must labour at governing; and a protest where employees follow rules exactly to reduce productivity.

clue.text: Offending rookie soon learned this was no local !

definitions.text: Offending rookie soon learned this was no local !

parts.words: Offending rookie soon learned this was no local !
parts.note: a misbehaving recruit is sent to a 'house' that turns out to be a military jail, not a pub

explanation.surface: A new recruit who breaks the rules quickly discovers the place he is sent to is no pub.
explanation.walkthrough: In British slang a local is one's neighbourhood pub, and a 'house' can be a pub; the military prison is nicknamed for its glass roof.
explanation.definitionFit: Glasshouse is British army slang for a military detention prison, from the glass-roofed Aldershot jail.

clue.text: Grim tourist's way to see the old city

parts.note: tourists 'do' a place when they visit its sights
Ur is the ancient Sumerian city in Mesopotamia

explanation.surface: A sour sightseer's approach to visiting an ancient city.
explanation.definitionFit: Dour is a synonym of stern, gloomy and severe.

clue.text: Irish female impersonator resisted eviction

parts.note: members of a 19th-century Irish secret society disguised themselves as women while fighting landlords' evictions

explanation.surface: An Irish drag artist who refused to be thrown out of his home.
explanation.walkthrough: The society was named for a widow said to lead the fight against evictions; members wore women's dress.
explanation.definitionFit: Member of a 19th-century Irish tenant society, active against landlords, whose men disguised themselves in women's clothes.

clue.text: One who draws part of a wedding-cake ?

definitions.meaning: someone who draws a game ties it, so is one who ties
a single stacked layer of a celebration cake

explanation.walkthrough: To draw a match is to tie it, so one who draws is, whimsically, one who ties.
explanation.definitionFit: Each layer of a stacked celebration cake is a level; and a person who ties a contest is jokily one who ties.

clue.text: Agreeing with eg the first letter of two

definitions.text: eg the first letter of two
definitions.meaning: the letter T, which opens the word two, is a non-vowel

explanation.walkthrough: The phrase 'consonant with' means in keeping with; T is a non-vowel letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Both senses: in accord or harmony with something, and a letter that is not a vowel, like T.

clue.text: Help us to change railway stuffiness?"

indicators.note: change says these three words are rearranged into a new order

explanation.surface: A plea to reform the railways' stuffy atmosphere.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stuffiness' looks like a stale atmosphere, but means stuffing: the padding in furniture.
explanation.definitionFit: Upholstery is the padding and covering of chairs and sofas, so it is the stuff in them.

clue.text: Ace pilot maybe going metric?

indicators.note: maybe says these letters could take another form, so rearrange them

explanation.surface: A flying ace adopting kilometres instead of miles.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Going metric' looks like decimal measures, but metric here means in metre, as verse is.
explanation.definitionFit: Poetical writing is in verse, so it uses metre and rhythm.

clue.text: Aircraft supplies top cover in German

indicators.note: in says the word for a top cover sits inside the abbreviation for German

parts.note: a lid is a cover on top of a box or pot

explanation.surface: A plane provides the top cover for a German.
explanation.definitionFit: A glider is an engineless aeroplane that flies on air currents.

clue.text: We hear the Arab chief is going — to get rid of someone?

indicators.note: we hear signals that the answer is said like the phrase that follows

parts.note: a sheikh is an Arab chief, and going means off

explanation.surface: Rumour says the Arab leader is leaving, perhaps to escape a pursuer.
explanation.definitionFit: To shake off a pursuer is to escape or lose them.

clue.text: " I am Sir —, And when I ope my lips let no dog bark ! " (Mer of Venice)

definitions.text: I am Sir —, And when I ope my lips let no dog bark !

parts.words: I am Sir —, And when I ope my lips let no dog bark !
parts.note: a quotation from Gratiano in The Merchant of Venice, mocking a pompous person who acts as an all-knowing prophet

explanation.surface: A pompous speaker demanding silence whenever he talks, in Shakespeare's words.
explanation.walkthrough: Fill the gap in Shakespeare's line: Gratiano mocks men who pose as infallible sages that everyone must hush for.
explanation.definitionFit: The quotation mocks a self-important man who acts like an infallible prophet whose pronouncements must not be interrupted.

clue.text: Coming event for, a right competitor '

parts.note: a rival is a competitor

explanation.surface: A forthcoming contest for a decent opponent.
explanation.definitionFit: An arrival is the event of someone or something coming.

clue.text: Substance mixed in — the chalice, Monsieur

indicators.note: mixed says the letters of the vessel and the abbreviation are stirred together

parts.note: M is the abbreviation for Monsieur, the French title

explanation.surface: Something stirred into the communion cup by a Frenchman.
explanation.definitionFit: A chemical is a substance made or used in chemistry.

clue.text: The syndicate has come about the wine container

indicators.note: about says the word come is wrapped round the storage word

parts.note: a bin is a rack or receptacle for storing bottles of wine

explanation.surface: A business group arrives to discuss the wine rack.
explanation.definitionFit: A combine is a group of businesses or people joined for a common purpose, like a cartel.

clue.text: Alumnus is to make arrangement for an instrumentalist

parts.note: an old boy (OB) is a former pupil of a school

indicators.note: make arrangement says the letters of the two words are reordered

explanation.surface: A former pupil is to arrange music for a performer.
explanation.definitionFit: An oboist plays the oboe, a woodwind instrument.

clue.text: Antelope bound to have lamb's tail all right

parts.note: to bound is to leap or spring

indicators.note: a word's tail is its final letter, so take the end of lamb

parts.note: OK means all right

explanation.surface: A leaping antelope must have a lamb's tail, and that is fine.
explanation.definitionFit: The springbok is a southern African gazelle known for leaping high.

clue.text: Yarn of a soldier-politician

parts.note: GI is an American soldier
MP is a Member of Parliament

explanation.surface: A story told by a man who is both soldier and politician.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Yarn' suggests a tale, but here it is a thread.
explanation.definitionFit: Gimp is a twisted trimming thread or cord used in upholstery and lace.

clue.text: Adversity's were sweet in Arden

parts.note: the exiled Duke in As You Like It, set in the Forest of Arden, praises the benefits of hardship

explanation.surface: Hardship turned out pleasant in the Forest of Arden.
explanation.walkthrough: Duke Senior's line: 'Sweet are the ___ of adversity'; Arden is the forest of As You Like It.
explanation.definitionFit: The Duke means hardship's benefits or purposes, the good ends it serves.

clue.text: The sin Gay called, a kind of praise

definitions.meaning: one of the seven deadly sins, coveting what others have

definitions.text: Gay called, a kind of praise
definitions.meaning: the poet John Gay wrote that this feeling is a kind of praise

explanation.surface: A poet describing one of the deadly sins as a form of compliment.
explanation.walkthrough: John Gay, author of The Beggar's Opera, wrote in his Fables that it 'is a kind of praise'.
explanation.definitionFit: Covetousness is one of the seven deadly sins; resenting another's success also flatters it, as Gay said.

clue.text: When one beginner returns in the pits, they're outnumbered

indicators.note: in says the reversed pair goes inside the word for pits

parts.note: mines are pits dug for coal or ore

indicators.note: returns says the words for one and beginner are read backwards together

parts.note: I is the Roman numeral one
a tiro is a novice

explanation.surface: A novice turning back down a coal mine, among the few.
explanation.walkthrough: I plus TIRO turned round gives ORITI, which goes into MINES.
explanation.definitionFit: Minorities are the smaller groups, outnumbered by the majority.

clue.text: Open-door university?

parts.note: an American Ivy League college that shares its name with a well-known make of door lock

explanation.walkthrough: The Open University is a British distance-learning institution; here the 'door' points to a lock brand.
explanation.definitionFit: Yale is an American university and also a brand of cylinder lock that opens doors.

clue.text: Fatal-drinks ?

parts.note: strong drinks that buck you up, read jokingly as ones that turn people into corpses

explanation.walkthrough: A 'stiff' is slang for a corpse, so a drink that makes stiffs would be fatal.
explanation.definitionFit: A stiffener is a strong alcoholic drink taken for courage; a stiff is slang for a dead body.
